standard.title: Create economic explanations
standard.description: create descriptions and explanations, using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms, and referencing information and data from sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can create descriptions and explanations using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms, and referencing information and data from sources (AC9HE7S05). At Year 8, the expectation develops toward explicit orientation of the audience to the issue and more deliberate use of data to support conclusions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions and explanations — using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms, and referencing information and data from sources — that orient an audience to an issue and support conclusions.

nodes.label: Orienting an audience to an issue
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a response that orients the audience to an economic or business issue using relevant concepts and terms, establishing what the issue is, why it matters, and to whom.
nodes.minimum_width: Write an opening for an explanation that orients the audience to one economic or business issue — identifying the issue, naming the relevant economic concept(s), and establishing why the audience should care.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a response that orients the audience (e.g. peers or community groups) to the issue using relevant economic and business concepts and terms such as 'markets', 'business', 'consumer and financial decision-making' and 'taxation'. Establish what the issue is, why it matters, and who is affected before moving to the explanation.
wider: Adapt the same explanation for two different audiences (e.g. peers vs parents vs community group) and analyse how the opening orientation needs to change to match audience knowledge, values and stakes
Practise issue orientation in different formats — a written paragraph, a spoken introduction, an infographic opening — and evaluate which elements are common to all formats and which vary
Research how economic journalists and public policy communicators orient audiences to complex issues (e.g. Reserve Bank explainers, ABS data stories) and identify the structural features they use
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot orient an audience to an issue tend to jump directly into their own knowledge or data, producing explanations that assume context the reader does not have. This undermines the communicative function of the entire response.

response_modes.reason: Audience orientation requires students to think about what the reader does not already know — a perspective-taking move that many Year 8 students have not yet internalised as a writing habit. Explicit scaffolding (write one sentence stating the issue; one sentence explaining why it matters; one sentence identifying who is affected) builds the habit before it is applied in a full piece.

success_criteria: Identifies the economic or business issue clearly in an opening that orients the audience
Names at least one relevant economics or business concept or term in the orientation

nodes.label: Using data and sources to support explanations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create a description or explanation that uses data or information from sources in appropriate formats to support decisions and conclusions about an economic or business issue.
nodes.minimum_width: Create an explanation of one economic or business issue that references at least one piece of data or information from a source, and explains how that data supports a conclusion.
nodes.typical_width: Create a description or explanation using data or information presented in appropriate formats to support decisions and conclusions about an economic and business issue. Reference sources accurately, explain the connection between the data and the conclusion, and use economic and business vocabulary accurately throughout.
wider: Create an explanation that integrates both qualitative information (case study, expert commentary) and quantitative data (statistics, trend data) — and analyses what each type of evidence contributes to the explanation

Produce an explanation in a data visualisation format (e.g. an annotated graph, an infographic with supporting text) and evaluate whether the format communicates the issue and evidence more or less effectively than prose

Evaluate an economic explanation produced by someone else (a news article, a student sample) against criteria: Does it orient the audience? Does it use concepts accurately? Does the evidence support the conclusion? Provide written feedback using those criteria

response_modes.reason: Creating evidence-referenced explanations improves through repeated practice across different issue types and formats. Students benefit from producing explanations of market issues, business strategy issues, and taxation/financial planning issues before formal assessment.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Communication is the synthesis skill of the entire inquiry cycle. Students who practise creating explanations across formats (written, visual, spoken) and audiences develop transferable communication capability that serves every subsequent year and subject that requires evidence-based explanation.
success_criteria: Creates an explanation that uses at least one piece of data or information from a source
Explains the connection between the cited data or information and the conclusion it supports
